# Your Field Card

<p class="hp-fc-lede">Twelve voyages on one page: the one thing to remember from each lab, its key takeaways, and the moves to make in your own Azure DevOps when you get back. Print it, or save it as a PDF (<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>P</kbd>), and pin it next to your monitor.</p>

## Day 1 · Charting the Waters

<p class="hp-fc-day">From Work Items to Management Intelligence</p>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 1</p>

### [Explore HarborPoint's Transformation Program](../day-1/lab-01-explore-the-program.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">The backlog order is the decision. When it disagrees with reality, don't quietly fix the list: find out who should decide, and ask them.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- The portfolio is a **ranked list**. When the rank and reality disagree, a decision is missing, so find out who should make it.
- Set up a Features backlog with **rollup columns** and you have Feature status for a whole Epic on one screen, with no work items opened.
- Use the right lens: the **backlog** for how far, the **form** for why, the **board** for where it's stuck, the **plan** for when.
- **Owns**, **serves** and **builds** are three different questions: Area Path, Parent link, and the children's areas. Cross-team Features hide in the gaps between them.
- Progress bars count only **Closed** work. Before you quote one, know what "done" means on that team's board.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Hold your ranking up to the light.** Open the Epics (or top-level) backlog your leadership treats as the portfolio, and lay it next to the last written priority list you were given. Write down every place they disagree, and who could settle it.
2. **Build your Feature status view once.** On your Features backlog, add **Progress by Story Points**, **Sum of Story Points** and **Progress by all Work Items**. Column settings are per user, so you change nothing for anyone else, and you'll never need a status spreadsheet for "how far along" again.
3. **Ask one team what "done" means.** Pick your most important Feature, find its owning team's board, and count the finished-but-not-Closed work. That's how much your progress bars are understating, or hiding.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 2</p>

### [The Monday Morning Manager Challenge](../day-1/lab-02-monday-morning-manager.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">Velocity tells you how busy a team was, not what it delivered. For every velocity number, ask which Features the points moved.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- Start wide: six teams' work at Feature level in one query, then zoom in on the team in question.
- Compare each team with **its own plan**. Velocity never compares across teams, and the gap between Planned and Completed is where carry-over hides.
- A Feature's progress bar doesn't tell you whether it will make its date. Where the remaining work is planned, what state it's in and who owns it does.
- Six signals find most of what needs a manager: unowned urgency, overload, stale work, mid-sprint scope, unaligned effort and quality debt. Each one is a two-clause query.
- **Feature progress is the truth serum for velocity.** Report what moved the portfolio, lead with the bottom line, and end with a specific ask.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Run two signals on the team you worry about most.** In **My Queries**, build open Priority 1 bugs with a blank `Assigned To`, and Active items with **Changed Date** `<` `@Today - 7`. My Queries is your private folder, so nobody sees your scratch work until you choose to share it.
2. **Read the gap, not the green.** Open that team's **Velocity** report from the **Analytics** tab, set **Velocity by** to **Sum of Story Points**, and compare **Planned** with **Completed** for each recent sprint. Your choice is saved for you only. Compare the team with its own plan, never with another team.
3. **Ask which Features the points moved.** Query last sprint's Closed user stories with **Iteration Path** `=` `@CurrentIteration - 1` for that team, and add `Parent` and `Story Points` columns. Add up the points with an empty Parent, and take that number to the team lead as a question, not a verdict.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 3</p>

### [Build Your Manager's Query Toolkit](../day-1/lab-03-query-toolkit.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">A saved query is a definition everyone inherits. Name it like the question it answers, and read the result before you forward it.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- A saved query is a **definition** everyone inherits. Name it like the question it answers and put the window in the name.
- Pick the query type for the question: **flat** for lists and charts, **tree** for "what does this work serve?", **direct links** for "what's missing or blocked?".
- `@CurrentIteration` picks a sprint, not a team. Pair it with an area clause, and check the team parameter.
- Trees hide orphans, and progress reports hide them too. Measure the gap between "work done" and "work that moved a Feature".
- Every result is a shortlist to read, not a verdict to forward. Test your zeros, distrust your tags, and triage before you escalate.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Save one question where others can find it.** Pick the question you're asked most, build it as a query, and save it in a **Shared Queries** folder where you have Contribute (ask your admin for one if you don't). Name it like the question it answers, minus the question mark. Shared queries are visible to everyone in the project, so a vague name misleads people you'll never meet.
2. **Find your team's orphan work.** Build a **Work items and direct links** query: one team's current-sprint user stories on top, `Work Item Type` `=` `Feature` below, **Only return items that do not have matching links**, and only **Parent** ticked. Whatever it returns is work no Feature report will ever show you.
3. **Define "at risk" once, on purpose.** Build one at-risk query with a grouped **Or** (a Target Date window with `@Today + n`, a Risk value, an `at-risk` tag) and put the window in its name. Then read every result before you send it to anyone.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 4</p>

### [The Sprint Delivery Report](../day-1/lab-04-sprint-delivery-report.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">A status color is only as good as the sentence next to it. Report what's left against the time left, and end with a decision you need.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- Charts work only on **saved, shared, flat** queries. Plan your evidence around what Azure DevOps can draw.
- Every chart answers one question. Decide your scope (area or Epic) and say it on the page.
- Compare each team with **its own plan**, never with another team's points.
- Counts, windows and percentages can all lie. Report **what's left against the time left**, over a window that fits the question.
- A status color is only as good as its evidence, and a status report is a request for decisions.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Chart one question from a shared query.** Take a saved flat query in a shared folder, open **Charts** › **New chart**, and name the chart for the one question it answers. Charts on **My Queries** are visible only to you, so save the query to a shared folder if anyone else needs to see it.
2. **Put each team next to its own plan.** Open each team's **Velocity** report, set **Velocity by** to **Sum of Story Points**, and note Completed ÷ Planned for recent sprints. Report that ratio and its trend, never one team's points against another's.
3. **Give your last status color a sentence.** Open the last status report you sent and write one line of evidence next to its RAG color. For each Feature on it, replace the percentage with what's left against the time left: remaining points and Target Date.

</div>

## Day 2 · The Lighthouse

<p class="hp-fc-day">Turning Information into Management Decisions</p>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 5</p>

### [Build HarborPoint's Management Command Center](../day-2/lab-05-command-center.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">A dashboard is a set of answers, not a set of widgets. If you can't say which question a widget answers, or its scope doesn't match the page, take it off.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- Design from questions. Five questions, each with someone who acts on the answer, decide which widgets earn a place.
- Every widget inherits a scope from its query or its team. Check it against the scope your dashboard's title promises, and put team names in titles.
- Pair a count with the list behind it. A risk tile starts a conversation; the list tells you which conversation.
- Managers need diagnostics; executives need decisions. Cut the exec view to a handful of widgets and say in words what the numbers mean.
- A dashboard is only as good as its upkeep: a named owner, a review date on the page, and the discipline to delete what you no longer maintain.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Write the questions onto the page.** Create a **project dashboard** of your own (Contributors can) and put a **Markdown** widget across the top: the owner, the five questions it answers, a review date and a color legend. Anyone who can see the dashboard sees it, so write it for them.
2. **Check every widget's scope.** On a dashboard you rely on, open the query behind each Query Tile and the **Team** setting of each Analytics widget, and compare them with the scope the page title promises. Fix the ones you own, put the team name in every team-scoped title, and send the owner a list of the rest.
3. **Pair your risk count with its list.** Save a shared, flat-list query of your at-risk Features, scoped with `Area Path` `Under` your own area. Give it a **Query Tile** with written color rules and a **Query Results** widget beside it, so the count always comes with the names.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 6</p>

### [Which Team Needs Help?](../day-2/lab-06-which-team-needs-help.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">Velocity measures estimates, not speed. Never judge a team on one chart: find three signals that agree, then change the system, not the number.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- Velocity is a team's sum of its own estimates. Pair it with throughput: rising points over flat counts is point inflation, not speed.
- Never reach a verdict on one chart. Look for three independent signals across output, flow and outcomes.
- Lower throughput with steady, reliable delivery is a capacity fact to plan around, not a problem to fix.
- The CFD shows where work waits, cycle time shows what the wait costs, and too much work in progress makes everything slower.
- Help means changing the system (WIP, intake, testing, quality bar), with an owner and a metric for each change. It never means a velocity target.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Read one team's velocity two ways.** On a team's backlog, open **Analytics** › **Velocity** › **View full report** and toggle **Velocity by** between **Sum of Story Points** and **Count of Work Items**. If points climb while the count stays flat, ask the team what changed in its estimates. Report settings are per user, so nobody else's view changes.
2. **Find where work waits.** Open the same team's **Cumulative Flow Diagram** with a **Custom rolling period** that covers the last five sprints, and look for a band that thickens. Then check its cycle time, and take what you find to the team as a question, not a verdict.
3. **Measure the work that serves no Feature.** In the Velocity report, select last sprint's **Completed** bar, add the `Parent` and `Story Points` columns to the query that opens, and add up the points with no parent. Do the same for a sprint five back, and see which way the share is moving.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 7</p>

### [The Cross-Team Bottleneck](../day-2/lab-07-cross-team-bottleneck.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">A plan with no red lines is not a plan with no risk. Most cross-team bottlenecks are priority decisions nobody made, so bring options and name who decides.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- A red line tells you two end dates disagree. It doesn't tell you why, how much, or what to do. That part is your job.
- Read dependencies at two altitudes. The Feature line shows the portfolio problem; the story links show the real handoff, which is often narrower, and narrower means more options.
- No line is not no risk. Plans draw only Predecessor/Successor links between dated items on the plan, so pair every plan with a direct-links query.
- Cross-team bottlenecks are usually portfolio conflicts in disguise. When mandatory work isn't ranked, the busiest team ranks it for you, and priority number one pays.
- Bring options, not alarms: each with its effect on the date, its risk, who pays and who decides.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Put your cross-team initiative on one plan.** **Boards › Delivery Plans** › **+ New plan**, add each contributing team at the **Features** level, and add a marker for the date that matters. Turn on **Show Parent**, **Show Tags** and **Show child rollup data**, then use **Show and hide dependencies** to draw every line. Look, don't drag: moving a card changes the real work item for everyone.
2. **Save a dependency query beside it.** Build a **Work items and direct links** query with `Parent` `=` your most important Feature's ID, **Only return items that have matching links**, and only **Predecessor** and **Successor** ticked. Add `Node Name` and `Iteration Path`, then look for any linked item with no sprint or from a team that isn't on your plan.
3. **Ask who decided.** Pick one red line, open the predecessor's **History** and filter **Fields** to `Target Date` to see who moved it and why. Then ask whose priority gave way, and whether that person was the one who chose.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 8</p>

### [The Executive Status Review](../day-2/lab-08-executive-status-review.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">Executives don't need everything you know. Give them the answer first, the two risks that matter, and a decision one named person can say yes or no to.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- Choose the argument before you build the dashboard. A good risk has a priority at stake, evidence, and a decision someone senior can make.
- An executive dashboard is an argument for a decision: few widgets, each tied to a question, each number with a threshold or a baseline.
- Translate metrics into member impact. "42 open bugs" means little to an Executive Committee. "Members are finding defects in production" means a great deal.
- Bottom line up front: the answer and the ask first, evidence second, every decision owned by one named person.
- Check how a number is made before you escalate it. The loudest chart in the room is often a data problem.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Put the bottom line on the page.** On the dashboard your sponsor opens, add a **Markdown** widget across the top with an "Updated:" date, a two-sentence bottom line, the decisions needed (each with one named decider) and your thresholds. Everyone who can see the dashboard reads it, so refresh it every week.
2. **Make bad news the default color.** On a Query Tile that tracks a problem, such as open P1 bugs, set **Default background color** to red and add one **+ Add rule** that turns it green at 0. When several rules match, the last one wins, so list them from mild to severe.
3. **Check how your loudest chart is made.** Pick the chart that gets the most attention in leadership meetings. If it counts completed work, open one recent sprint and look for items that are finished but not **Closed**, or have no Story Points, before anyone acts on the trend.

</div>

## Day 3 · Setting the Course

<p class="hp-fc-day">Planning Ahead and Connecting Delivery to Business Value</p>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 9</p>

### [Can HarborPoint Meet the Deadline?](../day-3/lab-09-meet-the-deadline.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">Velocity is a rate, not a promise. Subtract who's out and what's already committed, then answer 'can we?' with a range and a better option.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- Velocity is a rate for a normal sprint. Capacity is how much of it you'll actually get. Subtract absences, committed work and support load before you forecast.
- The forecast tool is a calculator: one velocity, backlog order and Story Points. It ignores in-progress work, sprint assignments and unestimated items, so feed it honest inputs.
- Order is scope. Moving one "should" below the MVP turned a miss into a fit without changing a single estimate.
- Forecast in ranges with conditions. A single date is a promise; a range is information a sponsor can act on.
- Never compare velocity across teams, and be wary of moving work to the "fastest" team. It's usually the busiest one.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Turn a velocity into a capacity.** For one team, read the average from **Analytics** › **Velocity** on its backlog, then open **Boards › Sprints** › **Capacity** for the next sprint. Subtract team days off, known absences, committed work and about 10% for bugs and support. You're only looking, so nothing changes unless you select **Save**.
2. **Run the forecast at two velocities.** On that team's **Stories** backlog, clear any filter, turn on **Forecasting** in **View options**, and run it once at the team's average and once at the capacity you just worked out. The gap between the two lines is your range. View options are yours alone, so nobody else's backlog changes, as long as you don't drag anything.
3. **Count the blanks before you quote a date.** In the Feature you're most likely to be asked about, count the stories with no Story Points: the forecast treats each one as free. Take that count and your range to the next "can we?" conversation, and ask who will size them this week.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 10</p>

### [One Service, Different Customer Needs](../day-3/lab-10-personas.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">The member doesn't see your org chart. A persona only changes what gets built when it reaches the acceptance criteria.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- A persona is a set of behaviors, goals and breaks backed by evidence. Mark everything else as an assumption.
- One service, many journeys. The breaks hide at the handoffs between channels, and those handoffs often fall between two teams' Features.
- Personas change what gets built only when they reach the acceptance criteria. One generic story usually serves one persona and fails the rest.
- Make prioritization arguable. A visible model turns "branch vs digital" into "which input is wrong?"
- Check the objective as well as the arithmetic. Counting heads through the door and counting relationship value give different orders, and choosing between them is a leadership decision.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Find a journey nobody owns.** Pick one service your customers use across two of your teams. Find the Feature each team owns for it on the Features backlog and open its **Links** tab. If there's no **Predecessor/Successor** link between them, the handoff has no owner: write down who should own it.
2. **Draft one persona page.** Under your own page in **Overview › Wiki**, use **Add sub-page** to start one persona with a **Quote**, **Goals**, **Frustrations**, **Needs from this service** and one journey break backed by a number you already have. Mark everything else *(assumption)*. Wiki pages are shared, so anyone on the project can read it and improve it.
3. **Rewrite one generic story with its Product Owner.** Find a story written for "the user" and, together, add Given/When/Then acceptance criteria for the person it would fail. Link it to your persona page from its **Links** tab (**Add link** › **Existing item** › **Wiki page**), and if you add a persona tag, agree the spelling first: tags can't be renamed or deleted in the web UI.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 11</p>

### [Why Is the Dashboard Wrong?](../day-3/lab-11-dashboard-wrong.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">When a team's numbers fall off a cliff, suspect the record before the team. A chart can be computed perfectly from data that is wrong.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- When a team's numbers fall off a cliff, suspect the record before the team. Delivery rarely collapses in one sprint. Hygiene often does.
- Fix data at the source. A query that compensates for bad data gets wrong in a new way each time the data changes.
- Typed-in sprints, "not Closed" for open, and single-spelling tags are the three most common query defects. Macros, explicit state lists and a written vocabulary prevent them.
- Every dashboard is a data-quality contract: an owner, defined terms, shared queries, and a weekly look at a watchlist whose healthy answer is zero.
- Governance has a cost and a reach. Team agreements are cheap and local. Process rules land on every project at once. Per-person hygiene scores get gamed.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Audit one tile before your next report.** Open the dashboard your leadership reads most, pick one tile, and read its query's **Editor** tab. Look for a sprint typed in by hand instead of `@CurrentIteration`, and "open" written as `State` `<>` `Closed`. Running a query never changes data.
2. **Build three queries whose healthy answer is zero.** Create a `Watchlist` folder and save: Active work with `Changed Date` `<` `@Today - 14`, stories in Resolved for more than 5 days, and anything filed at the project's root area. **My Queries** are private to you, so put the folder under **Shared Queries** if it will ever feed a dashboard tile, or everyone else sees an error instead of a number.
3. **Look at the counts with the team, not about the team.** Spend 15 minutes with one team lead and Product Owner going through the watchlist together. Anything above zero gets fixed on the spot or gets a named owner, and the counts stay team-level, never per person.

</div>

<div class="hp-fc" markdown>

<p class="hp-fc__num">Lab 12</p>

### [Capstone: The HarborPoint Management Challenge](../day-3/lab-12-capstone.md)

<p class="hp-fc__one">The data won't decide for you. Know who typed each number, speak in ranges, and get the right people to make the trade-offs on purpose.</p>

<p class="hp-fc__label">Key takeaways</p>

- A PI outlook is a set of bets with odds. Commit what's sized and staffed, make what depends on a decision conditional, and say plainly what can't be committed yet.
- Choose your instruments before you forecast. Inflated points, data defects and unsized Features flow straight into executive commitments.
- Capacity is gross throughput minus what's already spoken for: holidays, mandatory work, bugs and spill. Unreserved, it gets spent anyway.
- Value, member research and personas make trade-offs arguable. The deliverable is a decision with a cost and an owner, not a ranking.
- When the facts change mid-plan, update the plan. An outlook that can absorb a curveball is worth more than one that was right yesterday.

<p class="hp-fc__label hp-fc__label--harbor">Back in your own harbor</p>

1. **Choose your instruments.** For each team you report on, open **Velocity** in its **Backlogs › Analytics** and compare **Sum of Story Points** with **Count of Work Items**. Write one line per team: the throughput measure you'd forecast from, and the number you refuse to. Report settings are per user, so nobody else's view changes.
2. **Find the Feature with nothing inside.** On your Features backlog, add **Sum of Story Points** and **Progress by Story Points** from **+ Add a rollup column**, plus **Business Value** and **Effort** with **Column Options**. Any high-value Feature with no child stories or no Effort can't be forecast yet: note who should decompose it, and by when.
3. **Sort next quarter into three bands.** List the Features your leadership expects next, and put each one in **Committed**, **Likely** or **Not committed**. Beside every Likely item, write the decision or condition it depends on. That list is the first draft of your next outlook.

</div>
